strengths: AVIS addresses a meaningful gap between audio-visual semantic segmentation and video instance segmentation: distinguishing and tracking individual sounding objects, including instances of the same category. AVISeg provides a substantial resource with 926 videos averaging 61.4 seconds, 26 categories, and 94,074 instance masks, covering silent and overlapping-source situations.

The baseline has consistent support from established metrics. Under the stated common ResNet-50 backbone and training schedule, AVISM achieves 61.73 HOTA and 40.57 mAP, compared with 57.48/36.25 for VITA and 57.39/37.84 for COMBO (Table 2). These improvements support its usefulness independently of the proposed FSLA metric.

The ablations substantiate the audio-visual components. Adding video-level fusion to frame-level fusion improves HOTA from 59.59 to 61.73 and mAP from 39.06 to 40.57 (Table 4). Additional experiments examine window size, similarity loss, backbone, and pretraining.

The task illustrations and architecture diagrams communicate the approach clearly. The supplement documents training settings, baseline prompts, qualitative comparisons, and failure cases, and the manuscript supplies a dataset/code link. Taken together, the benchmark contribution and established-metric results support weak acceptance.
weaknesses: The FSLA specification contains consequential inconsistencies. Algorithm 1 increments the silent-frame correctness counter without checking for empty predictions, initializes counters outside the threshold loop, and omits explicit checks that object counts agree and every object matches. Its aggregation also does not implement the stated class averaging. These discrepancies prevent reproducing the reported FSLA values from the supplied algorithm. Separately, the claim that mAP does not penalize non-sounding predictions is too broad: such predictions can introduce false positives or reduce trajectory IoU.

The conclusions about multimodal large models exceed what their adaptations establish. Supplement E merges same-category masks into one identity for Sam4AVS and BuboGPT and treats each category as one instance for AL-Ref-SAM 2. Sam4AVS also selects only the top audio class. These choices structurally restrict instance separation and simultaneous-source coverage, confounding attribution of poor scores to the models' underlying reasoning capabilities.

Dataset quality assurance is insufficiently documented for the difficult audio-to-instance assignments. Section 4 reports repeated manual review but provides no quantitative agreement or audit results, nor detailed rules for ambiguous mixtures and sound transitions. The random video split is described without explaining source-level overlap checks. These are documentation and validation gaps; they do not establish that the annotations or splits are defective.

Evaluation does not isolate the task's defining same-category challenge. FSLAm combines all multiple-source frames, while Figure 10 explicitly shows failures involving multiple people, dogs, and tubas. Without a quantitative breakdown for these cases, the extent of progress on instance-specific acoustic association remains uncertain. Sampling at 1 FPS also limits conclusions about rapid changes in sounding activity.

Architectural originality is modest: object-token association and shifted-window temporal processing substantially follow Mask2Former and VITA. Table 5 demonstrates a window-size/capacity tradeoff, but provides no matched runtime or memory comparison against dense-feature alternatives. The strongest supported contribution is therefore the task and benchmark, with an effective incremental baseline; broader efficiency claims have limited experimental support.
